content.content:
### Ref-Based Storage

Ref-based storage (`git-refs`) is the default. It gives each new checkpoint its own Git ref, a named pointer inside your repository that Entire creates and manages for you. Each ref lives at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, and Entire saves and retrieves each checkpoint independently.

**The benefit:** With ref-based storage, pushes and reads stay fast even as your repository accumulates more agent history. Multiple agents can also save their work at the same time without competing to update a shared branch.

Ref-based checkpoints use 26-character, time-sortable ULIDs, such as `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`.

Ref-based storage first shipped as an opt-in option in Entire CLI 0.8.42 and became the default in 0.10.0, where `entire enable` writes it during a first-time setup and no longer asks you to choose.

### Branch-Based Storage

Branch-based storage (`git-branch`) keeps every checkpoint on a shared Git branch called [`entire/checkpoints/v1`](/glossary#checkpoints-branch). Each checkpoint sits at `<first two characters of the ID>/<rest of the ID>/` in the branch tree.

**The benefit:** All checkpoint history lives on one branch you can check out, browse, or clone like any other branch.

Branch-based checkpoints use 12-character hexadecimal IDs, such as `a3b2c4d5e6f7`.

A repository you enabled before Entire CLI 0.10.0 uses branch-based storage and stays on it until you [switch backends](#switch-backends).

<span />

## Find Which Backend a Repository Uses

The backend is named by `checkpoints.primary.type` in `.entire/settings.json`, or in `.entire/settings.local.json` when someone set it for their clone alone. An absent `checkpoints` block resolves to `git-branch`, which is why a pre-0.10.0 repository keeps branch storage without any setting naming it.

Checkpoint storage is ordinary Git, so Git reads it without Entire installed. List the per-checkpoint refs:

```bash theme={null}
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/
```

Each line names one checkpoint, where `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID and `<id>` is always the leaf. Check for branch-backed checkpoints too:

```bash theme={null}
git show-ref entire/checkpoints/v1
```

Output from both means the repository holds checkpoints in both formats, which is the expected state after a backend switch. To confirm what reached the remote, run `git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'`.

## Both Backends Stay Readable

Every reader routes by ID format, so one repository can hold both formats at once. This holds for the CLI, entire.io, and the Entire API.

| Checkpoint ID | Where the read goes |
| - | - |
| ULID | Refs only. ULIDs are minted only under ref-based storage |
| Hex, branch-based backend | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch |
| Hex, ref-based backend | Refs first, then the branch, since a hex checkpoint may still sit on the pre-switch branch |

`entire checkpoint list` merges both backends and de-duplicates by ID. A new checkpoint goes to the configured backend, while a backfill that adds a transcript, summary, or attribution to an existing checkpoint lands in whichever backend already holds it.

## Switch Backends

To enable ref-based storage in a new repository, run:

```bash theme={null}
entire enable --checkpoint-backend refs
```

To enable it in an existing Entire-enabled repository, run:

```bash theme={null}
entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
```

Both commands accept `refs` and `branch`, plus the canonical `git-refs` and `git-branch` that settings store. Add `--local` when the choice should apply only to your clone.

A switch applies to new checkpoints. Checkpoints written before the switch stay exactly where they are and keep resolving through the routing above, so `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain`, attribution, and entire.io continue to serve them. Entire deletes nothing during a switch, and your commands and commit workflow do not change.

Two things do change after a switch to ref-based storage. New checkpoint IDs become ULIDs instead of hex, and the pre-push hook starts pushing queued per-checkpoint refs instead of the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Leave that branch on the remote: it is where readers find every checkpoint captured before the switch.

## Migrate Existing Checkpoints into Refs

Migration is optional, since the routing above already resolves branch-backed checkpoints under a ref-based backend. Migrate when you want the whole history in one format, or when you want to stop carrying the v1 branch.

<Warning>
  Run the migration **before** you switch the backend to refs. The command refuses to run once ref-based storage is primary, because the refs are authoritative at that point and re-importing branch snapshots could only move them backwards.
</Warning>

```bash theme={null}
entire doctor migrate-checkpoints --dry-run
entire doctor migrate-checkpoints
```

The command wraps each checkpoint's current tree in a fresh commit and points its ref at it, keeping the hex ID as the ref name. It does not rewrite the branch commits, and it does not delete the branch. It skips checkpoints it has already converted, so you can re-run it after more branch activity.

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--dry-run` | Report what would be migrated without writing refs |
| `--remote NAME` | Push migrated refs to this remote instead of the checkpoint sync remote |

Migrated refs are queued for push. Run interactively, the command asks whether to push them now. Run without a terminal, it leaves them queued, and they flush on the next `git push` once ref-based storage is primary. Then switch and push:

```bash theme={null}
entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
git push
```

<span />

## Auto-Generate Checkpoint Summaries

Checkpoint metadata can carry a summary generated at commit time. Enable it with `strategy_options.summarize.enabled`:

```json .entire/settings.json theme={null}
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "summarize": {
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

Then choose the provider and model:

```bash theme={null}
entire configure --summarize-provider PROVIDER
entire configure --summarize-model MODEL
```

## Where Storage Settings Are Saved

toolUseResult.stdout:
### Ref-Based Storage

Ref-based storage (`git-refs`) is the default. It gives each new checkpoint its own Git ref, a named pointer inside your repository that Entire creates and manages for you. Each ref lives at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, and Entire saves and retrieves each checkpoint independently.

**The benefit:** With ref-based storage, pushes and reads stay fast even as your repository accumulates more agent history. Multiple agents can also save their work at the same time without competing to update a shared branch.

Ref-based checkpoints use 26-character, time-sortable ULIDs, such as `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`.

Ref-based storage first shipped as an opt-in option in Entire CLI 0.8.42 and became the default in 0.10.0, where `entire enable` writes it during a first-time setup and no longer asks you to choose.

### Branch-Based Storage

Branch-based storage (`git-branch`) keeps every checkpoint on a shared Git branch called [`entire/checkpoints/v1`](/glossary#checkpoints-branch). Each checkpoint sits at `<first two characters of the ID>/<rest of the ID>/` in the branch tree.

**The benefit:** All checkpoint history lives on one branch you can check out, browse, or clone like any other branch.

Branch-based checkpoints use 12-character hexadecimal IDs, such as `a3b2c4d5e6f7`.

A repository you enabled before Entire CLI 0.10.0 uses branch-based storage and stays on it until you [switch backends](#switch-backends).

<span />

## Find Which Backend a Repository Uses

The backend is named by `checkpoints.primary.type` in `.entire/settings.json`, or in `.entire/settings.local.json` when someone set it for their clone alone. An absent `checkpoints` block resolves to `git-branch`, which is why a pre-0.10.0 repository keeps branch storage without any setting naming it.

Checkpoint storage is ordinary Git, so Git reads it without Entire installed. List the per-checkpoint refs:

```bash theme={null}
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/
```

Each line names one checkpoint, where `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID and `<id>` is always the leaf. Check for branch-backed checkpoints too:

```bash theme={null}
git show-ref entire/checkpoints/v1
```

Output from both means the repository holds checkpoints in both formats, which is the expected state after a backend switch. To confirm what reached the remote, run `git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'`.

## Both Backends Stay Readable

Every reader routes by ID format, so one repository can hold both formats at once. This holds for the CLI, entire.io, and the Entire API.

| Checkpoint ID | Where the read goes |
| - | - |
| ULID | Refs only. ULIDs are minted only under ref-based storage |
| Hex, branch-based backend | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch |
| Hex, ref-based backend | Refs first, then the branch, since a hex checkpoint may still sit on the pre-switch branch |

`entire checkpoint list` merges both backends and de-duplicates by ID. A new checkpoint goes to the configured backend, while a backfill that adds a transcript, summary, or attribution to an existing checkpoint lands in whichever backend already holds it.

## Switch Backends

To enable ref-based storage in a new repository, run:

```bash theme={null}
entire enable --checkpoint-backend refs
```

To enable it in an existing Entire-enabled repository, run:

```bash theme={null}
entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
```

Both commands accept `refs` and `branch`, plus the canonical `git-refs` and `git-branch` that settings store. Add `--local` when the choice should apply only to your clone.

A switch applies to new checkpoints. Checkpoints written before the switch stay exactly where they are and keep resolving through the routing above, so `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain`, attribution, and entire.io continue to serve them. Entire deletes nothing during a switch, and your commands and commit workflow do not change.

Two things do change after a switch to ref-based storage. New checkpoint IDs become ULIDs instead of hex, and the pre-push hook starts pushing queued per-checkpoint refs instead of the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Leave that branch on the remote: it is where readers find every checkpoint captured before the switch.

## Migrate Existing Checkpoints into Refs

Migration is optional, since the routing above already resolves branch-backed checkpoints under a ref-based backend. Migrate when you want the whole history in one format, or when you want to stop carrying the v1 branch.

<Warning>
  Run the migration **before** you switch the backend to refs. The command refuses to run once ref-based storage is primary, because the refs are authoritative at that point and re-importing branch snapshots could only move them backwards.
</Warning>

```bash theme={null}
entire doctor migrate-checkpoints --dry-run
entire doctor migrate-checkpoints
```

The command wraps each checkpoint's current tree in a fresh commit and points its ref at it, keeping the hex ID as the ref name. It does not rewrite the branch commits, and it does not delete the branch. It skips checkpoints it has already converted, so you can re-run it after more branch activity.

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--dry-run` | Report what would be migrated without writing refs |
| `--remote NAME` | Push migrated refs to this remote instead of the checkpoint sync remote |

Migrated refs are queued for push. Run interactively, the command asks whether to push them now. Run without a terminal, it leaves them queued, and they flush on the next `git push` once ref-based storage is primary. Then switch and push:

```bash theme={null}
entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
git push
```

<span />

## Auto-Generate Checkpoint Summaries

Checkpoint metadata can carry a summary generated at commit time. Enable it with `strategy_options.summarize.enabled`:

```json .entire/settings.json theme={null}
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "summarize": {
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

Then choose the provider and model:

```bash theme={null}
entire configure --summarize-provider PROVIDER
entire configure --summarize-model MODEL
```

The `strategy_options` keys merge by layer as usual. See [Local, Project, and Global Settings](/guides/configuration/settings-layers) for the full table.

content.content: # Inspect Checkpoints in CLI Source: https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-cli List, explain, and measure checkpoints from a terminal. Use the Entire CLI when you want to work from a terminal, explain a checkpoint or commit, read transcript output, compare token usage, or export checkpoint data as JSON. ## Find a Checkpoint List checkpoints on the current branch: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint list ``` Add `--json` for a machine-readable listing, or `--session ID` to narrow the list to one session. When you do not know which checkpoint you want, search by phrase, meaning, or context: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint search "what changed" ``` ## Explain a Checkpoint or Commit Explain a checkpoint by ID, or by an unambiguous prefix of one: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint explain CHECKPOINT_ID ``` A commit-ish works too, and resolves through the commit's `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint explain HEAD~3 ``` Add `--full` for the whole parsed transcript, `--raw-transcript` for the JSONL file, or `--short` for the summary alone. ## Generate a Summary Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint explain CHECKPOINT_ID --generate ``` The `--generate` flag requires the configured provider CLI to be installed and authenticated. ## Measure Token Usage Report token usage and optimization recommendations for a checkpoint: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint tokens CHECKPOINT_ID ``` The report names the checkpoint, the sessions and agents behind it, the models they used, and the branch, followed by the usage breakdown and the recommendations drawn from it. It reads committed checkpoint metadata through the same resolution path as `entire checkpoint explain`, so an ID prefix or a commit-ish works here as well, and metadata missing locally is fetched from the checkpoint remote. Compare a checkpoint against an earlier one to see how usage moved: ```bash theme={null} entire checkpoint tokens CHECKPOINT_ID --compare BASELINE_ID ``` The comparison reports total tokens, input, cache and context replay, cache write, output, and API calls as a delta against the baseline, and qualifies whether the change counts as an observed reduction or increase. | Flag | Description | | - | - | | `--json` | Output the full report as JSON | | `--compare ID` | Compare against a baseline checkpoint | | `--agent-brief` | Print compact next-step guidance for an agent | `--json` and `--agent-brief` are mutually exclusive. ## Continue With Open checkpoint details, sessions, and file diffs visually. See the full checkpoint command reference. # Inspect Checkpoints in entire.io Source: https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-entire-io Open checkpoint details, sessions, and file diffs in entire.io. * checkpoint count, when more than one checkpoint is attached * author ## Checkpoint Detail Open a checkpoint to inspect the detail view. The header shows the commit SHA, branch, author, agent, file count, AI percentage, and token usage when available. The detail view has two main tabs: * **Sessions**: prompts, transcript, tool activity, session metadata, and any sessions that contributed to the checkpoint * **Changes**: modified files, with a file tree and diff view Use **Alt + Left Arrow** and **Alt + Right Arrow** to move to the previous or next checkpoint on the same branch. ## Open from a Commit You can open a checkpoint from a commit URL: ```text theme={null} https://entire.io/gh///commit/ ``` When a commit has an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, the checkpoint ID also appears in the commit message: ```text theme={null} fix: handle empty repos in dispatch generation Entire-Checkpoint: 01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN ``` You can also open a checkpoint from a session when that session produced or contributed to the checkpoint. ## Continue With List, explain, and measure checkpoints locally. See the transcript and tool calls behind a checkpoint. Answers to common questions about checkpoints and attribution. ## Checkpoints ### Why Does Entire Use Commit Trailers Instead of Git Notes? Entire links commits to checkpoints with an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer: ```text theme={null} Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7 ``` The trailer points to checkpoint metadata stored in your repository: one Git ref per checkpoint under `refs/entire/checkpoints/` by default, or the shared `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch in repositories that use the legacy branch backend. Entire uses this approach because commit trailers survive common Git workflows better than metadata attached only to a commit SHA. Git notes have a few practical limitations: * Normal Git pushes skip them unless you configure note refs separately * They attach to commit SHAs, which change during rebases, amends, and cherry-picks * Hosted Git platforms do not consistently support them in review and merge workflows By storing the stable checkpoint ID in the commit message, Entire keeps the link with the commit itself. That is more reliable for teams that rebase, amend, cherry-pick, use hosted merge flows, or have contributors using different Git clients.

content.content:
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo gh/owner/name
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo et/project/repo
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied,
                   including its subagent task records under "tasks".
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).

content.content:
- Connectors, by what they bring in:
  - Accounting: QuickBooks Online, Xero, NetSuite SuiteAnalytics.
  - Payroll and HR: around fifty, including ADP Workforce Now, Gusto,
    Rippling, Deel, Workday, BambooHR, Paychex, Paylocity, Justworks,
    TriNet, Personio and HiBob.
  - CRM: Salesforce, HubSpot.
  - Spreadsheets: Google Sheets.
  - Databases: PostgreSQL, including Amazon RDS, Aurora and Google
    Cloud SQL.
  - Files: CSV and raw file upload, which is not a billable
    integration.

  The live catalogue in the product is the authority and is longer
  than any list written down here. Accounting and databases are the
  classes worth naming exactly; the payroll and HR set is broad enough
== integrations/integrations-directory    17639
15:* **Standard**: QuickBooks Online, Xero, Rippling, Google Sheets, and many more.
22:**CSV / Raw File Upload** is a manual option for bringing in a raw file directly. Use it when a live connection is not set up yet, or for a one-off or specialized report a system does not sync automatically. File upload is not a billable integration.
41:A workspace holds one QuickBooks Online company and one Xero organisation at a time. Connecting a second one reports that the integration's connection limit is reached. If you run more than one legal entity and want the group in a single Model now, export the second entity's ledger and bring it in through **CSV / Raw File Upload**, then give the Model an Entity Dimension so you can report on each entity and on the group. [Dimension mappings](/formulas/core-concepts/dimension-mappings) covers landing two entities' account structures in one reporting structure. Ask Ari what your own workspace allows before you plan around the limit.
70:* **Google Sheets** (Standard)
73:Use a Google Sheets connection when a Variable is still maintained in a spreadsheet outside your other systems. You sign in with Google and pick one spreadsheet in Google's file picker; cfo.ai reads only the files you pick and keeps no copy of the files themselves; the data Ari imports from a file is stored in your Model like any other import. **Google Drive** works the same way for one Google Sheet, Excel workbook, or CSV file. Ari imports the file as it would an upload, and the connection re-reads it on the nightly refresh and when you ask Ari to refresh it. A Google Sheet is read as an Excel workbook of up to 50 MB; an Excel or CSV file stored in Drive is read up to 10 MB, and a larger one is not imported until it is made smaller. Every Google Sheets connection in a workspace shares one plan slot, while each Google Drive connection takes a slot of its own; your workspace's Usage settings show which class your plan gives each. See [Connect a Google Sheet or Drive file](/integrations/connect-and-sync-data#connect-a-google-sheet-or-drive-file).
84:A cloud data warehouse is not one of them. Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and Databricks are not sources you can connect today. To model curated warehouse datasets now, land them in a PostgreSQL-compatible database cfo.ai can read, or export them and bring them in through **CSV / Raw File Upload**.
135:Connected integrations refresh once a day, automatically. By default every integration, whether it is QuickBooks Online, Xero, NetSuite, Google Sheets, or a database, refreshes in one shared nightly run that starts at 02:00 UTC and finishes within a few hours, so your Actuals are fresh by the start of the US workday.
== integrations/connect-and-sync-data    28452
18:* A Google Sheet, a file in Google Drive, or a PostgreSQL-compatible database.
19:* A CSV or another supported file-upload flow for a source that is not connected directly.
23:A file you upload as a data source must be a CSV with a `.csv` extension, up to 50 MB. An uploaded Excel workbook is not accepted as a data source: attach it to a chat message for Ari to read, ask Ari to [import it as a model](/getting-started/import-a-spreadsheet-model), or connect it through [Google Drive](#connect-a-google-sheet-or-drive-file), which imports a workbook the way Ari imports an upload.
61:* **Integrations** lists the business systems cfo.ai can import from, with a **Connect** button on each card and an **Upload** button for CSV files.
87:## Connect a Google Sheet or Drive file
89:**Google Sheets** and **Google Drive** are listed under **Data upload** on the **Integrations** tab. Select **Connect** on the card: a Google sign-in opens, then Google's own file picker, where you choose one file. The Google Sheets picker shows spreadsheets; the Google Drive picker also shows Excel workbooks and CSV files. The card reports **Opening Google authentication…**, **Choosing in Google…**, **Completing connection…**, and then **Connected**. Closing Google's picker without choosing a file closes the flow with no error; the connection stays unfinished, shows **Setup not finished**, and offers **Finish setup**. Google grants cfo.ai access to the files you pick and nothing else in your Drive, and you can revoke it from your Google account.
96:A Google Sheet is read with every tab, its formulas, cached values, and number formats, and Ari rebuilds it the way it rebuilds an uploaded workbook. Each sync compares the file with the last import and does nothing when it is unchanged; a changed file starts an update of the Model. A Google Sheet is read as an Excel workbook of up to 50 MB, and an Excel or CSV file stored in Drive up to 10 MB. A larger file shows **This file is too large to import. Make it smaller and the next sync imports it.**, and in a chat Ari names the limit that applied, such as the 50 MB cfo.ai attaches as an Excel workbook. One connection reads one file, and the same file cannot be connected twice in a workspace. A Google Sheets or Google Drive connection made earlier through Fivetran keeps syncing as it did.
100:If you attach a CSV in Ari chat, choose whether it should become a data source or stay attached only to the conversation.
131:Each column a query returns loads into the Model as a Variable or a Dimension. cfo.ai guesses the role when the column first loads: a numeric column becomes a summed Variable unless its name marks it as an identifier: a name that ends in the word "id", including a camel-case ending such as `dealId`, or in "account number" or "account code", such as `Customer ID`, `deal_id`, `P&L Account Number`, or `SalesDefaultAccountCode`. Such a column loads as a text Dimension, so a leading zero in `00400` and every digit of a long ID stay as written, while `Account Balance` and `Number of Accounts` still sum. A column a database or warehouse query returns as text (`TEXT`, `VARCHAR`, `STRING`, or `CHAR`) loads as a text Dimension whatever its name and even when every value looks like a number, so a cast in the saved SQL, such as `to_varchar(stage_order)`, chooses the role before the first load; text whose values are all dates still loads as dates. Columns returned as numbers, and untyped CSV columns, still follow the name rule. An identifier that loaded as a number before these rules keeps its stored type. If a code loaded as a summed Variable, ask Ari to load it as a Dimension instead. Ari switches the role in place, so formulas, tables, and filters that already point at the column keep working, and every later load keeps the new role. A switched column keeps its stored type, so a number column that becomes a Dimension has number items; to keep leading zeros, return the column as text under a new name. A column that loads into a Dimension other queries also feed, such as four QuickBooks connections' **Customer** columns feeding one Customer Dimension, cannot have its role switched for one query: Ari names the shared Dimension and the other queries instead.
149:A source that syncs through Fivetran, such as NetSuite, HubSpot, Salesforce, a database, or a Google Sheets connection made earlier through Fivetran, stays connected when a sync fails on the provider's side. The connection reads **cfo.ai lost access** only when the provider asks for a new authorization. cfo.ai retries the sync on the next nightly run, and you can ask Ari to retry it now.

5:> One line: **`git bisect` for agent behaviour, with receipts.** Give Culprit a good ref, a bad ref and an eval suite. It finds the commit that broke your agent, explains *why* that change was made (from the Entire session), writes the smallest fix that restores quality while keeping the intended gain, and proves it statistically.
17:**Why now:** Coding agents write a growing share of agent code. Entire captures the session intent behind each commit, and neatlogs captures the traces of every agent run. Culprit is the first workflow that joins **intent (Entire) + behaviour (neatlogs) + statistics** to answer "what broke, why, and how do we fix it without losing the gain?"
34:5. **G5** — Deep, natural use of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, with a measured v1 → v2 improvement of Culprit itself.
46:| **The agent (30%)** | Plans a search, uses tools (git, worktrees, eval runner, neatlogs readback, Entire CLI), keeps state (SQLite ledger), recovers (skip/resample/resume/budget), verifies (CI-based decision + held-out suite) |
47:| **Required tools (25%)** | neatlogs and Entire are *inputs to the product*, not decoration; cfo.ai is fed measured cost-per-bisect from the ledger |
50:| **Usefulness/originality (10%)** | Real, recurring pain for the exact audience of neatlogs/Entire |
52:**Mandatory submission items** (from neatlogs.com/hackathon): demo video ≤ 3 min covering all three tools · cfo.ai business plan · before/after run with compared numbers · neatlogs traces/screenshots · Entire checkpoints (link + ID) · a run showing recovery from a failed action · public share links tagged #neatHack · public repo with commits dated during the hackathon · X quote-post of the official neatlogs post with team name, project name, repo and demo.
57:2. *As an agent engineer*, I see each tested commit's pass rate with a 95% Wilson interval, cost and latency, plus links to the neatlogs traces of the failing runs.
58:3. *As an agent engineer*, I read *why* the culprit commit was made (the Entire session prompt/summary) next to the diff.
60:5. *As an agent engineer*, if Culprit is killed mid-run, `culprit resume <run_id>` continues without re-running completed work.
71:- neatlogs tracing of every victim run and of Culprit's own reasoning; trace links in the report.
72:- Entire checkpoint context for the culprit commit (with a documented fallback).
76:- Cost export (CSV/Google Sheet) for cfo.ai.

5:> One line: **`git bisect` for agent behaviour, with receipts.** Give Culprit a good ref, a bad ref and an eval suite. It finds the commit that broke your agent, explains *why* that change was made (from the Entire session), writes the smallest fix that restores quality while keeping the intended gain, and proves it statistically.
17:**Why now:** Coding agents write a growing share of agent code. Entire captures the session intent behind each commit, and neatlogs captures the traces of every agent run. Culprit is the first workflow that joins **intent (Entire) + behaviour (neatlogs) + statistics** to answer "what broke, why, and how do we fix it without losing the gain?"
